lesson.title: Grading Efficiency: Power Factor
lesson.summary: Power factor is the ratio of real power to apparent power, a single number that grades how efficiently a circuit converts the current a source supplies into useful work.
lesson.body:
Power factor answers a single, practical question: of all the apparent power a source must supply, what fraction actually does useful work? It is defined as the ratio of average, real, power to apparent power, pf = P/S, and because P = Vrms Irms cos θ while S = Vrms Irms, the Vrms Irms terms cancel, leaving simply pf = cos θ. Power factor is a dimensionless number between 0 and 1, or, as a percentage, between 0% and 100%, with no unit of its own, since it is a ratio of two quantities already measured in watts and volt-amperes.

A power factor of 1.0 means every volt-ampere the source supplies converts to real power, only possible in a purely resistive circuit where θ = 0°. A power factor of 0 means none of the apparent power converts to real power at all, only possible in a purely reactive circuit where θ = ±90°. Real loads, motors, transformers, most industrial equipment, sit somewhere in between, and because cos θ is the same for +θ and −θ, power factor alone does not reveal whether current lags or leads voltage; the label lagging or leading must be attached separately to remove that ambiguity.

For the series RL circuit, P = 172.8 W and S = 288 VA, so pf = 172.8/288 = 0.6000. Equivalently, using the impedance angle θ = 53.13° directly, pf = cos(53.13°) = 0.6000, the same result. Since this is an RL, inductive, circuit, current lags voltage, so the power factor is reported as 0.6 lagging, not merely 0.6.

A low power factor is expensive even when no extra real power is being used, because it forces a utility's generators, transformers, and wiring, all sized in terms of apparent power, to carry more current than the customer's actual energy use would suggest. A factory drawing 172.8 kW, scaling the example up by 1000, at 0.6 lagging power factor demands 288 kVA of generation and delivery capacity, nearly 1.67 times what a purely resistive 172.8 kW load would need; many commercial electricity tariffs penalize customers directly for a poor power factor. This economic pressure is exactly what drives power factor correction, the deliberate addition of reactance, usually capacitive, to cancel out an inductive load's lagging angle, the subject of the final section on leading power factor.

Power factor also has a direct geometric meaning in terms of impedance: since θ is the impedance angle, cos θ = R/|Z|. For the series RL circuit, R = 30 Ω and |Z| = 50 Ω, so pf = 30/50 = 0.6000, the same value found from P/S. This makes intuitive sense: the larger the resistive fraction of an impedance is compared to its total magnitude, the closer the power factor sits to 1, and the more of the circuit's apparent power converts into real, usable work rather than being tied up in reactive energy that merely oscillates back and forth between source and load without ever being consumed.
